architectural_implications.before: Traces, logging, and evals added after launch in response to incidents.
architectural_implications.consequence: Debugging and cost attribution for multi-turn loops become tractable, but harness scope expands and eval coverage becomes a launch-blocking dependency.
architectural_implications.observation: Observability and evaluations are positioned at the top of the AgentCore architecture rather than as a peripheral tooling layer.

architectural_implications.after: Agents own provisioning via IaC, with policy and identity bounding what they can create.
architectural_implications.before: Humans provision cloud resources through consoles; agents only invoke APIs at runtime.
architectural_implications.consequence: Authorization and plan-review mechanisms become the critical safety surface; the object under review shifts from runtime calls to generated infrastructure plans.
architectural_implications.observation: Deployment moves from human clickops to infrastructure-as-code generated and managed by agents.

architectural_implications.after: Settlement and authentication live beside memory, runtime, and tools in the harness.

architectural_implications.observation: Payments and identity are modeled as harness components rather than application-level concerns.

architectural_implications.after: Framework-provided per-tenant isolation and secure memory on deployment.
architectural_implications.before: Prototype agents with a single user, local state, and no isolation boundary.
architectural_implications.consequence: The framework/CLI layer becomes the enforcement point for tenant boundaries, so framework version and config correctness carry security weight.
architectural_implications.observation: Multi-tenant isolation and secure memory are handled by CLI scaffolding rather than application code.

project_ideas.measurement: Number of unsafe plans blocked, false-positive rate on benign plans, reduction in simulated blast radius (resources affected), and added approval latency per plan.
project_ideas.name: Agent IaC Plan Gate
project_ideas.poc: Build an agent that generates infrastructure-as-code plans; enforce policy checks (deny public buckets, wildcard IAM, destructive replacement) and require human approval on plan diffs; run adversarial and benign plans through the pipeline.

project_ideas.hypothesis: Scoping an agent's identity to a spend-limited wallet with per-transaction and aggregate limits, enforced at runtime, prevents runaway spend while allowing legitimate microtransactions, and does so with acceptable false-positive rates.
project_ideas.measurement: Prevented unauthorized spend (absolute and percentage), false-positive rate for legitimate transactions, audit completeness (every transaction traceable to identity and policy decision), and policy decision latency.
project_ideas.name: Identity-Bound Wallet Scoping
project_ideas.poc: Implement an agent with a scoped wallet, policy engine (limits, merchant allowlist, velocity checks), and audit log; simulate a mix of legitimate purchases and adversarial attempts (limit evasion, replay, spoofed identity).

project_ideas.based_on: CLI tools simplify scaffolding multi-tenant agent applications with secure memory and tool integration.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Multi-tenant isolation provided by CLI scaffolding (e.g., AgentCore) is enforced at a specific boundary (process, container, memory store, API) and can be verified by adversarial cross-tenant probes; leakage is possible when isolation relies on application code rather than runtime enforcement.
project_ideas.measurement: Number of successful cross-tenant accesses (leakage incidents), isolation boundary failure rate, and time-to-detect leakage across probe types.
project_ideas.name: Cross-Tenant Leakage Test Suite for Scaffolded Agents
project_ideas.poc: Deploy two tenants using the same scaffolded agent framework with shared infrastructure (e.g., common memory store, vector DB, tool registry); attempt to read or mutate other tenant's memory, secrets, or tool outputs via prompt injection, API parameter tampering, and direct store access.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Mike Chambers
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Harness engineering and building production-ready AI agents on AWS
  • Purpose: To educate AI engineers on harness engineering, explaining the difference between using agents and building production agents at scale using AWS infrastructure, Strands Agents SDK, and AgentCore. Mike Chambers, Senior AI Specialist Developer Advocate at AWS, discusses harness engineering—the code, configuration, and execution logic that surrounds an AI model to make it production-ready. He contrasts agents we use (like coding assistants) with agents we build, introduces the Agentic AI Foundation, and demonstrates building and deploying agents using Strands Agents SDK and AgentCore.

Topic Map

Introduction and Background

  • Explanation: Mike Chambers introduces himself, his background at AWS, and his work on generative AI courses, MCP lambda handlers, and the Agentic AI Foundation.
  • Key claims:
    • AWS is a founding member of the Agentic AI Foundation within the Linux Foundation.
    • Chambers worked on deep learning courses with Andrew Ng reaching hundreds of thousands of enrollments.
  • Examples:
    • Building MCP lambda handler generating 35k downloads a month.
  • Terminology:
    • AWS
    • Agentic AI Foundation
    • Strands Agents SDK
  • Why it matters: Establishes speaker credibility and context around enterprise AI development.

Agents We Use vs Agents We Build

  • Explanation: Distinguishing between off-the-shelf consumer agent tools we use (like Claude Code, Cursor, Kiro) versus agents engineered and built internally for production workloads.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents we use rely on token maximization and local workflows.
    • Agents we build require structured harnesses, memory management, security, and scalability.
  • Examples:
    • Cursor and Claude Code as agents we use.
    • Custom enterprise agent applications built using AgentCore.
  • Terminology:
    • Agents we use
    • Agents we build
    • Token maxing
  • Why it matters: Highlights why software engineering best practices apply differently to agentic architectures.

Defining Harness Engineering

  • Explanation: Defining agent harness: Agent = Model + Harness. Harness engineering is the practice of engineering everything around the model.
  • Key claims:
    • A harness is every piece of code, configuration, and execution logic that is not the model itself.
    • Agent minus model equals harness.
  • Examples:
    • LangChain and Martin Fowler/Birgitta Böckeler definitions of agent harness engineering.
  • Terminology:
    • Harness engineering
    • Agent harness
  • Why it matters: Provides a clear mental model for separating base LLM capabilities from application scaffolding.

Components of an Agent Harness

  • Explanation: Breakdown of the various components required in a robust production agent harness.
  • Key claims:
    • Observability and evaluations must be prioritized first.
    • Harness components include loops, scaling, memory, identity, skills, tools/mcp, runtime, security, payments, and context management.
  • Examples:
    • Connecting to documentation servers via MCP servers.
  • Terminology:
    • MCP
    • Observability
    • Context management
    • Evaluations
  • Why it matters: Outlines the comprehensive architecture needed to scale agents beyond local experiments.

Live Coding and Deployment Demo with Strands and AgentCore

  • Explanation: Demonstrating local agent creation using Strands Agents SDK and AWS AgentCore CLI tools.
  • Key claims:
    • Strands Agents SDK allows rapid local prototyping of agents with tools and memory.
    • AgentCore provides CLI and infrastructure-as-code capabilities for deploying agents at cloud scale.
  • Examples:
    • Running python scripts with uv run and testing agent responses locally.
    • Using agentcore create and agentcore dev to spin up a web UI inspector.
  • Terminology:
    • Strands SDK
    • AgentCore
    • uv run
    • Multi-tenant isolation
  • Why it matters: Shows practical implementation of harness engineering using modern open-source tooling.

Key Points

Agent = Model + Harness

  • Explanation: The core formula defining an AI agent, where the model provides intelligence and the harness provides execution logic, tools, memory, and guardrails.
  • Evidence: Referenced articles by Birgitta Böckeler and Martin Fowler.
  • Practical implication: Engineers should focus development effort on building robust harnesses rather than training base models.

No more slop ops

  • Explanation: Moving away from ad-hoc manual console clicking (clickops) toward infrastructure-as-code managed by agents.
  • Evidence: Chambers' advocacy for infrastructure-as-code agent deployments.
  • Practical implication: Production agents must build and manage their own cloud infrastructure safely.

Observability and evaluations first

  • Explanation: Tracking traces, logging, and evaluation metrics should be foundational elements in agent harness design.
  • Evidence: Placement of observability and evaluations at the top of the AgentCore architecture diagram.
  • Practical implication: Without robust observability, debugging complex multi-turn agent loops at scale is impossible.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

AgentCore Architecture Framework

  • How it works: Provides modular components for building, deploying, and assessing production agents at cloud scale.
  • Components:
    • Harness (CLI, strands, models, tools, skills, memory)
    • Built-in tools (browser, code interpreter, knowledge base, search)
    • Gateway (APIs, lambda functions, configuration bundles)
    • Policy (authorization control)
    • Runtime (agents, tools)
    • Identity (inbound and outbound authentication)
    • Payments (automated microtransactions)
    • Registry (agents, MCP servers, tools, skills)
    • Memory (short and long term memory)
    • Observability and Evaluations
  • When to use: When deploying domain agents into enterprise production environments on AWS.

Examples & Case Studies

Building a simple calculator and time-checking agent in Python using Strands SDK.

  • Illustrates: How minimal boilerplate is needed to define tools and system prompts in a modern agent framework.
  • Lesson: Basic prototypes are easy to build locally, but production scaling requires dedicated harnesses.

Using AgentCore CLI to initialize an agent project, configure memory, model selection, and deployment options.

  • Illustrates: Automated provisioning of infrastructure-as-code for agent runtimes.
  • Lesson: CLI tools simplify scaffolding multi-tenant agent applications with secure memory and tool integration.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Distinguish clearly between consumer agents you use and production agents you build.
    • Explore Strands Agents SDK on GitHub for building model-first agent applications.
    • Utilize AgentCore for AWS agent deployments and infrastructure management.
  • Strategic:
    • Prioritize harness engineering over model fine-tuning for most application use cases.
    • Implement multi-tenant isolation and session management early in agent architecture.
    • Treat observability and evaluations as core requirements, not afterthoughts.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do different agent frameworks handle multi-turn context persistence at enterprise scale?
    • What are the best practices for securing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers in production?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • AWS is a founding member of the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. (organizational fact)
  • Strands Agents SDK supports Python and TypeScript with model-first design. (technical feature)

Notable Quotes

"A harness is a set of straps and fastenings used to control an animal..." (at 6:42) "The term harness has emerged as a shorthand to mean everything in an AI agent except the model itself." (at 7:00) "agent minus model equals harness." (at 8:05) "I don't want to see any more slop ops." (at 10:22)

Compressed Summary

  • Agent harness engineering encompasses all code, tools, memory, and orchestration surrounding an LLM.
  • Distinguishes agents we use interactively from agents we engineer and build for production.
  • Strands SDK provides a fast open-source framework for building Python and TypeScript agents.
  • AWS AgentCore enables secure cloud-scale agent deployment, session management, and multi-tenant isolation.
  • Keywords: harness engineering, agents, aws, mcp, agentcore, strands
  • Core insight: Harness engineering—managing memory, tools, loops, and infrastructure around an LLM—is the critical discipline for deploying production-grade AI agents at scale.

- **Why it matters**: Shows practical implementation of harness engineering using modern open-source tooling.
## Key Points
### Agent = Model + Harness
- **Explanation**: The core formula defining an AI agent, where the model provides intelligence and the harness provides execution logic, tools, memory, and guardrails.
- **Evidence**: Referenced articles by Birgitta Böckeler and Martin Fowler.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers should focus development effort on building robust harnesses rather than training base models.
### No more slop ops
- **Explanation**: Moving away from ad-hoc manual console clicking (clickops) toward infrastructure-as-code managed by agents.
- **Evidence**: Chambers' advocacy for infrastructure-as-code agent deployments.
- **Practical implication**: Production agents must build and manage their own cloud infrastructure safely.
### Observability and evaluations first
- **Explanation**: Tracking traces, logging, and evaluation metrics should be foundational elements in agent harness design.
- **Evidence**: Placement of observability and evaluations at the top of the AgentCore architecture diagram.
- **Practical implication**: Without robust observability, debugging complex multi-turn agent loops at scale is impossible.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### AgentCore Architecture Framework
- **How it works**: Provides modular components for building, deploying, and assessing production agents at cloud scale.
- **Components**:
  - Harness (CLI, strands, models, tools, skills, memory)
  - Built-in tools (browser, code interpreter, knowledge base, search)
  - Gateway (APIs, lambda functions, configuration bundles)
  - Policy (authorization control)
  - Runtime (agents, tools)
  - Identity (inbound and outbound authentication)
  - Payments (automated microtransactions)
  - Registry (agents, MCP servers, tools, skills)
  - Memory (short and long term memory)
  - Observability and Evaluations
- **When to use**: When deploying domain agents into enterprise production environments on AWS.

### Building a simple calculator and time-checking agent in Python using Strands SDK.

- **Lesson**: Basic prototypes are easy to build locally, but production scaling requires dedicated harnesses.

- **Illustrates**: Automated provisioning of infrastructure-as-code for agent runtimes.
- **Lesson**: CLI tools simplify scaffolding multi-tenant agent applications with secure memory and tool integration.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Distinguish clearly between consumer agents you use and production agents you build.
  - Explore Strands Agents SDK on GitHub for building model-first agent applications.
  - Utilize AgentCore for AWS agent deployments and infrastructure management.
- **Strategic**:

  - Implement multi-tenant isolation and session management early in agent architecture.
  - Treat observability and evaluations as core requirements, not afterthoughts.

- Distinguishes agents we use interactively from agents we engineer and build for production.
